candidates.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
candidates.raw_excerpt: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth . The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse. Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.) Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun . A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams. candidates.raw_excerpt: Credit: ESA / S. Corvaja / Andrew Parsonson (edit) Italian rocket manufacturer Avio has revealed that delays in the delivery of customer satellites have pushed the third Vega C launch of 2026 back toward Christmas, several weeks later than previously planned. Speaking during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on 11 November, Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo explained that the mission, which will carry six satellites, had been delayed as the company awaited the arrival of the final spacecraft. “The satellites from the customers are a little bit late, so we are waiting for the last few of them to arrive,” said Ranzo. “It’s an interesting mission, six different satellites. They’re coming in a little bit late, so we are coming very close to Christmas Day.” During the company’s half-year earnings call on 10 September, Ranzo said that the mission was scheduled for “the very beginning of December”. Based on his latest comments, the launch appears to have slipped by approximately two to three weeks. The flight is expected to carry six satellites for Italy’s IRIDE Earth observation constellation. According to photographs published by the French space agency CNES, a shipment of the Thales Alenia Space-built satellites arrived in French Guiana by air on 9 November 2026. candidates.title: ULA Set to Return Vulcan to Flight in First Amazon Leo Launch
candidates.raw_excerpt: United Launch Alliance is set to return its Vulcan rocket to flight this weekend in its first launch for the Amazon Leo constellation. The Vulcan rocket has been out of service since February, when it experienced an anomaly with the solid rocket motors built by Northrop Grumman. The February launch for the U.S. Space Force as a customer was successful, but the Space Force suspended Vulcan launches for the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) program to fix the anomaly. ULA recently stated that after an investigation with its team, Northrop Grumman, the Space Force, and government agencies, changes to the nozzle were made and fully tested. Vulcan has only launched a total of four times, including its debut mission in early 2024 . The Amazon mission is set to launch on Saturday, Nov. 14 at 12:32 p.m. ET from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. It was delayed by one day due to a power interruption in the air liquide gaseous nitrogen (GN2) plant, which ULA stated resulted in the loss of their high-pressure pumps. The mission will launch 40 Amazon Leo satellites — the largest launch yet for Amazon leo. The rocket is configured in the Vulcan VC6L variant with the Centaur V shorter, optimized version of the upper stage and six side-mounted solid rocket boosters. This marks the first of 38 Vulcan rocket launches for Amazon, following eight missions for Amazon Leo with the Atlas V rocket. Amazon Leo Launch Systems Director Melissa Wuerl said this starts a “sprint” of Vulcan launches. “Larger rockets and more frequent launches are critical to scaling our constellation and getting service to customers, and the Vulcan program is designed to deliver on both dimensions,” said Melissa Wuerl, director of launch systems for Amazon Leo. “Vulcan will launch close to half our first-generation constellation, making it our primary workhorse over the next several years.” The post ULA Set to Return Vulcan to Flight in First Amazon Leo Launch appeared first on Via Satellite .

Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 90 minutes prior to launch. It will be caught by the launch tower’s robotic arms, known as the ‘chopsticks’. If all goes according to plan, it will mark the first time a Version 3 Super Heavy Booster has returned to the pad. Three previous boosters were caught by the launch pad tower. If Ship 42 vehicle successfully reaches orbit and SpaceX mission control deems it healthy, it will remain in space for up to 14 orbits of the planet, before making its own return to the launch site, 22.5 hours after launch or at around 3:17 p.m. CST (4:17 p.m. EST / 2117 UTC). SpaceX has options to end the mission early with splashdowns off Hawaii and Chile if there is any doubt about the safety of a landing attempt at Starbase, which will take the craft over Mexico and South Texas. If both stages return successfully, it would be the first full recovery of an orbital launch system. SpaceX said on its website that would be “a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket.”

candidates.raw_excerpt: Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand. I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. I look away, look back and begin again. This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky. The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up. But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. candidates.title: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
candidates.raw_excerpt: Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star. The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153. GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs. The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR) "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself." candidates.title: The Microsoft outage China barely felt: A lesson on data sovereignty
candidates.raw_excerpt:
Microsoft's latest failure was global in reach, but not global in impact.

From around 4.17 p.m. UTC on Thursday, the US tech giant's services including Outlook, Teams, Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot, were degraded for more than 10 hours. The disruption reached at least 74 countries, with Outlook complaints on Downdetector – a third-party outage-monitoring platform that aggregates user reports – peaking near 140,000. 

The damage was heavily concentrated in the Americas, Europe and Australia. Governments didn't treat it as a purely private-sector issue. Germany's federal cybersecurity authority, BSI, said it was in contact with Microsoft and that "numerous companies" had been cut off from core cloud services. Australia's Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said he had activated a mechanism requiring Microsoft to prioritize the country's recovery, after both the Australian Federal Police and the domestic intelligence agency ASIO confirmed they were hit. Japan's government said its shared administrative IT backbone, GSS, was disrupted forcing some ministries back to phone communication. The Philippines' Supreme Court warned that email responses and online transactions would be delayed.

China sat in a blank space on that map. 

Why China was unfazed 

Multinationals in Shanghai on Microsoft's global platform were hit, as were Chinese exporters whose partners live on Outlook. Some foreign firms and foreign-related personnel in China using the global version were still affected. But the broader country didn't blink.

candidates.raw_excerpt: Europe continues to stack the building blocks for a more robust space economy.  Gama, a French startup developing ultra-light deployable solar arrays, announced a €15M seed round yesterday to boost Europe’s solar array supply chain. The round included funds from a mix of European and US VCs, including Transition Ventures, Planet A, Draper Associates, and Manta Ray. The funds will be used to develop a high-volume production facility outside of Paris, France, which will be capable of producing 100 MW of solar arrays annually. The first units—called Wings—are expected to start rolling off the line next year. Gama also plans to hire ~60 employees in engineering roles across mechanical, electrical, and software. The tech: Gama was initially founded to develop solar-sail technology—which uses the Sun’s energy to propel spacecraft into deep space—but the company quickly transitioned into developing solar arrays to solve the ever-present supply-chain headache for other satellite operators. Nearly every spacecraft in orbit relies on solar panels to power its payloads, but solar cells are built by a small number of providers and can often come with lead times as high as a year or more, according to CEO Andrew Nutter. Additionally, as power needs increase, the size of the solar arrays required to run each satellite grows larger, causing them to become floppy—and less effective at gathering sunlight. While traditional solutions involve adding weight to increase rigidity, Gama’s solution uses software—uploaded into customer flight computers—to help point the solar arrays at the Sun, and to solve the floppy-disk problem without additional mass. “Our approach is to make [solar arrays] as thin and light as possible, so you can have more surface area, and you reduce the cost and the mass. candidates.title: Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
candidates.raw_excerpt: A satellite looks down at the International Space Station in orbit. (Image credit: HEO) A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above. What is it? Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments. But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory. HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range. This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO . So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024). Why is it incredible? While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface. A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

Shares in the company have also plummeted by nearly 50 percent since June, the FT notes, as ratings downgrades and rising skepticism over the viability of the AI industry scare investors into safer corners of the market. In order to keep pumping money into AI powerlabs like OpenAI, SoftBank itself has started digging into junk bonds — high-risk debt, essentially — raising over $11 billion in non-investment grade bonds in September. So on top of boasting perhaps one of the highest degrees of exposure to the AI bubble on the planet, the Japanese investment firm is now the world-record holder for the largest corporate junk bond offering ever made. candidates.title: China unveils MAZU weather early warning device at COP31

China unveiled a compact weather early warning device at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 11, sharing its technology to help prevent and reduce the impact of weather-related disasters.

The device, part of China's MAZU intelligent early warning solution, was introduced through a promotional video at the High-Level Forum on South-South Cooperation on Climate Change.

Combining hardware and software in a single unit, it is designed to help developing countries deploy MAZU locally and readily incorporate data from their own weather observations.

The unit integrates data storage, AI processing, networking, display and computing functions, and supports Ethernet, 5G and satellite communications.

Its tools include forecasts for the immediate hours ahead and the short term, a dashboard providing an overview of key information, operational monitoring and on-site AI assistance.

The device can operate independently on site or connect to cloud resources and work with existing operational systems. It also supports modular expansion and ongoing upgrades, helping countries quickly strengthen their early warning capabilities.

As of October 2026, the broader MAZU solution had been deployed in eight countries, including Pakistan, Ethiopia and Sri Lanka, with cloud-based trials underway in more than 50 countries. It provides a public service for disaster prevention and risk reduction worldwide, helping strengthen local capabilities.
